questions.stem: The Ramsar Convention on Wetlands was signed in 1971 at:
questions.explanation: The Convention was signed on 2 February 1971 in the Iranian city of Ramsar on the Caspian Sea — hence the name. It came into force in 1975. 2 February is observed as World Wetlands Day. India joined in 1982 and — as of early 2026 — has over 85 Ramsar sites, the largest network in Asia.

questions.stem: Chilika Lake — the largest brackish-water lagoon in India — lies in which state?
questions.explanation: Chilika — on the east coast in Odisha — was India's first Ramsar site (1981). Area ~1,100 km² (varies seasonally). Home to the Irrawaddy dolphin, vast flocks of migratory birds, and the endangered Barkudia limbless skink. Removed from the Montreux Record in 2002 after successful rejuvenation — a rare success story cited at international forums.

questions.stem: The 'Montreux Record' maintained under the Ramsar Convention is a list of:

options.option_text: Wetlands of international importance under threat
Wetlands that have lost their protected status

questions.explanation: The Montreux Record (established 1990) is a register of Ramsar-listed wetlands where ecological character has changed, is changing, or is likely to change due to pollution, human interference, or other factors. India currently has two sites on the Record — Keoladeo National Park (Bharatpur, Rajasthan) and Loktak Lake (Manipur). Chilika was the only site ever removed (2002) after restoration.

questions.stem: Loktak Lake — famous for its floating 'phumdis' (vegetation masses) — is situated in:
questions.explanation: Loktak — the largest freshwater lake in North-East India — is in Manipur. Its phumdis host Keibul Lamjao National Park, the only floating national park in the world, and the last habitat of the Sangai (Rucervus eldii eldii), Manipur's state animal (also called the dancing deer or brow-antlered deer). Loktak is on the Montreux Record due to siltation and the Ithai barrage's ecological impact.

questions.stem: Keoladeo National Park — a Ramsar site and UNESCO World Heritage site — is located in:
questions.explanation: Keoladeo (formerly Bharatpur Bird Sanctuary) — Bharatpur, Rajasthan — is a man-made wetland created by the Maharaja of Bharatpur in the 19th century. Winter home to thousands of waterfowl; was the only known wintering site of the Siberian crane in India (last confirmed sighting 2002). Declared a National Park in 1982, UNESCO World Heritage site 1985, Ramsar site 1981. Currently on the Montreux Record over water-shortage issues.

questions.stem: Wetlands are often called the 'kidneys of the landscape' because they:
questions.explanation: Wetlands trap sediments, absorb excess nutrients (nitrogen, phosphorus), and break down pollutants through microbial action — similar to kidneys filtering blood. Other ecosystem services: flood control (storm-water buffer), groundwater recharge, carbon sequestration (mangroves, peatlands store huge carbon), biodiversity refuge, fisheries support, shoreline stabilisation. 'Kidneys of the landscape' is a phrase coined by American ecologist William J. Mitsch.

questions.stem: Under the Wetlands (Conservation and Management) Rules, 2017, the authority responsible for notifying and managing wetlands at the state level is the:
questions.explanation: The 2017 Rules — replacing the 2010 rules — decentralised management. Each State / UT sets up a State Wetland Authority (SWA), chaired by the environment minister, to identify and notify wetlands, regulate activities, and maintain a Brief Document per wetland. Prohibited activities: conversion for non-wetland uses, setting up / expanding industries, solid-waste dumping, untreated effluent discharge. The National Wetland Committee (under MoEFCC) provides oversight.
